blocks.text: Matter exists in four states: solid, liquid, gas and plasma. The simplest form of matter is the gaseous state, and most of the matter around us is solid. Liquids are less common than solids, gases and plasmas, because the liquid state of any substance exists only within a relatively narrow range of temperature and pressure. The kinetic molecular theory of gases helps to understand the properties of gases, liquids and solids.

items: Gases have no definite shape or volume; the volume of a gas is the volume of its container.
Ideal gases have zero particle volume.

The molecules of a gas are widely separated and most of the volume of a gas is empty space (nearly 99.9 per cent), which is why gases are compressed easily. When a gas expands suddenly, cooling takes place: the Joule-Thomson effect.
The pressure of a gas is due to the collisions of its molecules with the walls of the container.
There are negligible intermolecular forces in ideal gases.

blocks.alt: Three boxes of particles: a few blue dots flying freely in the gas box, closely packed blue dots in the lower part of the liquid box, and a purple grid of dots in the solid box, each with its properties listed below. Underneath, two pairs of containers show air halving its volume when the pressure doubles while water hardly changes.
blocks.caption: Particles in a gas, a liquid and a solid, and the effect of doubling the pressure (original diagram after Figure 5.1 and the printed property lists).
blocks.long_description: In a gas the molecules are far apart, so the gas fills its container, is almost all empty space and compresses easily; its pressure is the drumming of molecules on the walls. In a liquid the molecules touch but move past each other, so the volume is fixed, the liquid flows and diffuses, and it compresses very little. In a solid the particles are packed in place and only vibrate. Doubling the pressure halves the volume of air but shrinks water by only 0.0045 per cent.
